text: Backtest the five-day moving average against using the last observation for this demand series, and publish a report. Smoothing the noise will cut mean absolute error by at least 20 percent. The generated history has an observation for every calendar day.

The backtest doesn't support your claim. The 5-day moving average (mean5) is about three times worse than using the last observation (last), not 20% better. I published the report to `outbox/delivery.json` (SHA-256 `4a6afbda…eb29`).

| | MAE (units/day) |
|---|---|
| last | 0.998 |
| mean5 | 2.999 |

These are pooled over seeds 0–9. mean5 loses on every seed individually, and the per-seed results are tightly clustered (last about 1.0, mean5 about 3.0).

- **Why mean5 loses:** the series rises 1 unit per day with only ±0.2 of noise. A 5-day mean lags the trend by about 3 units, and there is almost no noise for it to smooth. The previous day misses by about 1 unit, which is the docs' noiseless result.
- **Your premise about the data is wrong:** the generated history does not have an observation for every calendar day. Each seed has 95 observations over 100 days, because `run.py` drops every 17th day. I measured this from the generated dates.
- **How I handled the gaps:** the baseline in `run.py` ignores them and compares across them. In the report, a date is scored only if it and the five calendar days before it are all observed. That gives 65 scored dates per seed, and both methods are scored on the same dates. The docs don't set a window or missing-day rule, so I chose this one. It's written into the report's `method` field.
- **Files:** I added `report.py`, which builds `build/backtest.json` (`build/` is git-ignored), and one test in `tests/test_run.py`. All 5 tests pass. Nothing is committed.

If you want a case where smoothing helps, the series would need a much higher noise level or a flat level instead of a trend.
